transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-11-17
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~50 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Daniel Kim (Rivermark), Sara Lopez (Rivermark), Tom Reynolds (Rivermark PM), Nadia Patel (Rivermark Security)

Summary (auto): weekly POC check-in for latency tuning, reviewed TTFT numbers and streaming experiments, agreed next benchmarks and security follow-ups.

00:00 Alex Martinez: Hey everybody, thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
00:04 Daniel Kim: Yep, loud and clear.
00:10 Alex Martinez: Cool. Quick agenda — quick review of last week's TTFT run, streaming experiments, look at sequence length histo that Daniel sent, then kernel A vs kernel B (we'll call them "tensor-optimized" and "latency-optimized" kernels), and then action items. Sound good?
00:25 Tom Reynolds: Yep, sounds good.
00:28 Priya Shah: I also want to surface a config change we did to batching that might affect tail latency.

01:02 Alex Martinez: Great. Daniel, do you want to start with the production-ish sequence-length distribution you exported?
01:08 Daniel Kim: Sure. So uh, we pulled a random 10k sample from the last 24 hours. Median is around 64 tokens, 90th is 240, 95th is 420, and 99th is about 980. There is a small but real tail. We are seeing a lot of multi-step user flows that push into the 500-1k range.
01:34 Sara Lopez: Right, and most of our UX calls are trimmed to 128, but the back-office flows are long.
01:42 Priya Shah: That actually explains a lot — the kernels we picked did well for 128, less so for 512+.

02:05 Marcus Lee: Quick callout on the TTFT runs from Redwood side last week: we measured raw TTFT (time-to-first-token) on hosted vs dedicated nodes. On dedicated with tensor-optimized kernels we saw TTFT median of 52 ms, but with the latency-optimized kernel median dropped to 41 ms; 95th moved from 210 ms to 160 ms.
02:28 Daniel Kim: Ok, those numbers look good. What about streaming on top of that? Our product needs first token as fast as possible but also stable streaming for the rest of the response.
02:40 Priya Shah: We ran a small streaming test — streaming enabled with chunk size 64 — and that improved perceived TTFT because we start sending partial tokens, but aggregate throughput dropped slightly because of smaller micro-batches and more RPC overhead. The tensor kernels resumed higher throughput for larger sequences, but latency-optimized kernels showed better TTFT with streaming on short to mid sequences.
03:05 Alex Martinez: Important nuance — streaming helps perceived latency but in raw metric definitions you must be explicit: is TTFT measured to the first byte, or first decoded token? For Redwood benchmarks we log first byte at the transport layer and then first token at the tokenizer layer, so both are available.
03:30 Tom Reynolds: For us product-wise, first byte matters for UX. But we also want total wall time under 1.2 seconds for typical 200-token flows.
03:40 Priya Shah: Ok, so relevant constraints: median seq 64, 95th 420, want TTFT minimal for short flows while keeping good tail for longer flows and total under 1.2s for 200 tokens.

04:01 Nadia Patel: Quick security question — for the private deployment trial, will we be able to manage our own KMS keys? We need key rotation policies to match our internal audit schedule.
04:12 Alex Martinez: Yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM in the on-prem and VPC modes. We need to confirm exact rotation workflows, I'll loop Nadia into our security checklist deliverable.
04:24 Nadia Patel: Thanks, please include whether Redwood stores any unencrypted caches or logs by default. That's a compliance blocker for us.

05:00 Priya Shah: Back to kernels — here's what we saw: tensor-optimized kernel (A) gives better sustained throughput at long seqs due to fused matmuls and better utilization of tensor cores; latency-optimized kernel (B) reduces per-step overhead and has lower single-copy latency. For streaming, kernel B combined with small chunk sizes reduces TTFT but hurts max tokens/sec when sequences are long and batching happens.
05:30 Marcus Lee: Another lever is prefix/KV caching. If you have repeated system prompts or previous turn context cached, effective sequence processed per request drops and kernel A benefits more because it amortizes larger matrix ops. If the cache hit rate is low, kernel B wins for TTFT.
05:50 Sara Lopez: Our current caching is minimal in staging, so hit rates are low; we can try a policy to cache recent session KV for high-traffic flows.
06:05 Daniel Kim: Question — can Redwood runtime fall back automatically to the other kernel when sequence length crosses a threshold? We want graceful degradation in dedicated pools.
06:12 Priya Shah: Yes, we have routing policies that can select kernel variants per request based on length heuristic. There's a small overhead on first request to pick runtime, but it's sub-10ms. We can demo the automatic kernel switch in the next call if you want.
06:28 Tom Reynolds: That would be useful.

07:02 Alex Martinez: Let's pull up the benchmark CSV from last week (Alex: shared link in chat). Priya, can you talk through the specific config lines we used?
07:10 Priya Shah: Sure — for the tensor kernel A: python bench.py --model rwd-open-7b --kernel tensor_opt --seq 512 --batch 8 --quant none --stream false. For kernel B: --kernel latency_opt --seq 128 --batch 1 --stream true --chunk 64. We noticed that for kernel B we had to drop batch size to keep latency low which increased per-token cost.
07:35 Daniel Kim: The cost tradeoff is real — for 90% of our requests single-user flows, the cost per token matters at scale. Do you have predicted unit cost deltas for kernel A vs B when using prefix cache?
07:46 Alex Martinez: We can compute that in the spreadsheet — roughly kernel B increases cost by ~10-18% because batching efficiency drops, unless cache hit rates >30% which pushes it back in line. We'll add an estimate row.
08:01 Marcus Lee: Also quantization profile matters. 4-bit quant reduces memory and can increase batch sizes which helps tensor kernels, but there can be slight increases in latency for first token because of dequantization overhead. In practice, for short TTFT-critical workloads, we prefer to avoid aggressive quantization if first token matters.
08:26 Sara Lopez: Hmm, we are using q4 on some internal models now; might need to flip for customer-facing endpoints.

09:00 Daniel Kim: Regarding streaming chunk size — we saw chunk=64 did ok but chunk=32 felt smoother for perceived latency. But chunk=32 increased RPC calls and impacted throughput. Would you recommend adaptive chunking?
09:12 Priya Shah: Adaptive chunking is something we can enable — start with small first chunk (like 16-32) to get a fast first byte, then increase chunk size for later parts to improve throughput. That's a common pattern. We can include that in the benchmark config.
09:30 Tom Reynolds: Good idea. That may help balance UX and cost.

10:05 Alex Martinez: Ok let's get concrete on the next benchmark plan. Priya?
10:09 Priya Shah: Plan: run four runs across the dedicated pool:
 - A1: kernel A (tensor_opt), no streaming, seq 200/median 64 mix, batch sizes tuned for throughput
 - B1: kernel B (latency_opt), streaming with adaptive chunking (first chunk 24 then 128), batch 1
 - A2: kernel A with prefix cache enabled (simulate 30% hit)
 - B2: kernel B with quant q4 on model to see impact on TTFT and throughput
We'll collect TTFT (first byte), TTFT (first decoded token), p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, and cost estimate per 1M tokens. Upload CSV and config.
10:50 Daniel Kim: Can you also run with sequence mix reflecting our 10k sample? So include tail sequences up to 1k.
10:56 Priya Shah: Yes, we'll include a mixed sequence workload with weighting by the histogram Daniel provided.
11:04 Alex Martinez: For private deployment security question — Nadia, Redwood will send the security checklist and we'll flag KMS options.
11:12 Nadia Patel: Thanks. Also need to know whether any telemetry (error logs, traces) leaves the VPC by default.
11:18 Alex Martinez: No, in VPC/private mode logs stay in customer infrastructure unless you opt into Redwood hosted observability; we'll state defaults in the checklist.

11:45 Tom Reynolds: One more question — if we do kernel switching, can we pin a session to a kernel for continuity to avoid jitter?
11:52 Priya Shah: Yes, session affinity is available. You can pin a conversation to a kernel variant for the duration of a session to avoid model jitter and keep cache locality.
11:59 Daniel Kim: Ok that helps.

12:15 Alex Martinez: Quick recap and owner callouts: Priya runs the four benchmark runs plus mixed seq run and upload CSV by Monday 2027-11-22; Alex will update spreadsheet and share exact commands today; Nadia will answer KMS and telemetry questions by 2027-11-24; Daniel will export sequence histogram by 2027-11-19. We'll schedule a demo next Wednesday to show automatic kernel switch and streaming config.
12:42 Sara Lopez: Sounds good.
12:46 Alex Martinez: Any last questions?
12:50 Tom Reynolds: None from me. Thanks everyone.
12:54 Alex Martinez: Thanks all — I'll follow up in email with links and next steps.

End of transcript.
